_source: SevenNova orchestrator — LAMC Title 12 base density rules (simplified, by-right only, no ADU bonus). Mirrors worker/src/orchestrator.ts maxUnitsByRightCalc.

zones.name: R1 — One-Family Dwelling Zone
zones.density_rule: 1 primary dwelling per lot. SB 9 (2021) allows a second unit and/or urban lot split on most R1 parcels, and California ADU law adds an ADU + JADU.
zones.units_formula: 2 units typical ceiling by-right (house + SB 9 second unit), plus ADU/JADU under state law
zones.typical_use: Single-family homes, SB 9 duplex conversions, ADU additions
zones.developer_note: R1 is where SB 9 lot splits and ADU strategies create value. A standard R1 lot can often support a main house, an ADU, and a JADU — three rentable units where zoning maps say one.

zones.name: R2 — Two-Family Dwelling Zone
zones.density_rule: 1 unit per 1,500 sq ft of lot area under LAMC Title 12.
zones.typical_use: Duplexes, small multifamily, owner-occupied + rental combinations
zones.developer_note: R2 lots near transit can stack TOC bonuses on top of base density. A 7,500 sq ft R2 lot in a TOC Tier 3 area supports 7 units by-right + bonus.

zones.name: R3 — Multiple Dwelling Zone
zones.density_rule: 1 unit per 800 sq ft of lot area under LAMC Title 12.
zones.typical_use: Apartment buildings, condo developments, small-lot subdivisions
zones.developer_note: R3 is LA's workhorse multifamily zone. With TOC Tier 4 (+80%), a 7,500 sq ft R3 lot reaches 16 units — the math that drives most Westside apartment development.

zones.name: R4 — Multiple Dwelling Zone (High Density)
zones.density_rule: 1 unit per 400 sq ft of lot area under LAMC Title 12.
zones.typical_use: Mid-rise apartments, mixed-income projects, ED1 100%-affordable developments
zones.developer_note: R4 + ED1 (100% affordable) unlocks ministerial approval with the +80% state density bonus — no Planning Commission hearing, 6-14 month timelines instead of 2-4 years.

zones.name: R5 — Multiple Dwelling Zone (Maximum Density)
zones.density_rule: 1 unit per 200 sq ft of lot area under LAMC Title 12.
zones.typical_use: High-rise residential, downtown towers, transit-adjacent density
zones.developer_note: R5 is concentrated in Downtown, Century City, and along major corridors. Base density is rarely the constraint — height districts and FAR govern the real envelope.

zones.name: RD1.5 — Restricted Density Multiple Dwelling
zones.density_rule: 1 unit per 1,200 sq ft of lot area under LAMC Title 12.
zones.developer_note: RD zones were designed to step down density between R3 corridors and R1 neighborhoods. RD1.5 at 1,200 sq ft/unit often pencils for townhome product where R2's 1,500 doesn't.

zones.name: RD2 — Restricted Density Multiple Dwelling
zones.density_rule: 1 unit per 1,200 sq ft of lot area under LAMC Title 12 (shares RD1.5's per-unit minimum; differs in lot-area minimums).
zones.developer_note: RD2 parcels cluster in Mid-City and the Valley. Same per-unit density math as RD1.5 — value differences come from lot minimums and neighborhood context.

zones.name: RD3 — Restricted Density Multiple Dwelling
zones.density_rule: 1 unit per 1,200 sq ft of lot area under LAMC Title 12.
zones.developer_note: RD3 reads like RD1.5/RD2 on density but typically carries larger minimum lot sizes — check the specific tract before underwriting unit count.

zones.name: RD4 — Restricted Density Multiple Dwelling
zones.density_rule: 1 unit per 1,600 sq ft of lot area under LAMC Title 12.
zones.developer_note: RD4's 1,600 sq ft/unit makes fourplexes the natural product on standard lots — a configuration lenders underwrite as residential, not commercial.

zones.name: RD5 — Restricted Density Multiple Dwelling
zones.density_rule: 1 unit per 2,000 sq ft of lot area under LAMC Title 12.
zones.developer_note: RD5 sits one notch above duplex density. Triplex product on a 7,500 sq ft lot — often the highest count achievable without discretionary review.

zones.name: RD6 — Restricted Density Multiple Dwelling
zones.density_rule: 1 unit per 2,400 sq ft of lot area under LAMC Title 12.
zones.developer_note: RD6 is the gentlest multifamily step above single-family — duplex-scale product that neighborhood councils rarely contest.
